summary:
Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program. The Human Dignity Trust records the Barbados case as one of a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes across the Eastern Caribbean. A High Court ruling on sodomy, published May 2023, found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is documented and recent enough to matter. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward and suffered serious injuries including to her throat. Coward was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or face three months in prison; reporting through Maurice Tomlinson and the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network records that no jail time was handed down. A visibly trans visitor who is assaulted should not expect a custodial sentence against the attacker.

Legal gender recognition does not exist as a sourced entitlement. Identity-document processes and legal gender recognition for trans Barbadians are not covered by the available material, so a visitor should assume no mechanism exists to align documents with presentation, and should carry whatever home-issued identification matches how they present.

Employment protection stops short of trans people. The Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars employment discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status. Trans activist Alexa D.V. Hoffmann argues the Act excludes trans workers because gender identity and gender expression are not listed as protected grounds. Reporting from August 2020 states that trans Barbadians are frequently fired or denied jobs for 'dressing wrong'.

No same-sex relationship is recognised. In June 2016 the government ruled out changing the law to allow same-sex marriage; in September 2020 it announced only a plan to recognise 'some form' of civil union, to be followed by a referendum on gay marriage. Critics called the civil union proposal 'unnecessarily vague' and assessed the referendum as likely to fail; neither measure had been enacted as of the source's account. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by law, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families. The only parenting-related service identified is the Barbados Fertility Centre, which offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.

The state has treated LGBT emigration as presumptively abusive. In 2011 the government said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada, and in 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean expressed concern that such applications were an attempt to abuse the Canadian refugee system, noting two of nine Canadian applications had been denied. A 2016 Guyanese newspaper reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the UK and the US, and UGLAAB said it would investigate the same allegations. Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category. The July 2020 'Welcome Stamp' remote-work visa initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse before being changed to permit same-sex spouses.

Official and religious hostility is prominent in the public record. In 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite stated Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and after UK Prime Minister David Cameron's 2011 CHOGM aid warning about sodomy laws he said publicly that Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a 'cheap political trick' since its report did not mention same-sex marriage. Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued that discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and human rights activists report that more American evangelical ministers arriving in Barbados have spread homophobic rhetoric more widely.

In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154, ss.9 and 12), and the IACHR gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019. Failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision.

Trans people on the island are visible and exposed at once. The second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil in Barbados was held in November 2018, organised with NOW, a local ally and veteran trans advocates, and Hoffmann's first-person account of that period describes both visibility and danger. Barbados Gays, Lesbians and All-Sexuals Against Discrimination (BGLAD), founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed, was set up to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue, and Pride events (a first small event in November 2017 and a parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown, in July 2018) have served an awareness-raising function.
tangentialFactors:
The decriminalisation of December 2022 belongs to a wider Eastern Caribbean pattern of colonial-era anti-gay statutes falling to constitutional litigation rather than to parliamentary repeal, and the Barbados case sits in that series alongside challenges in neighbouring islands. A trans visitor should note that the pattern's driver is litigation over sexual conduct between men; it does not by itself produce gender-identity protections, and Barbados's employment and family law have not followed.

Public rhetoric runs well behind the litigation outcome. The Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church oppose the buggery law while respecting LGBT rights, and PM Mia Mottley, elected May 2018, is reportedly 'pro-LGBT', but the same period produced the attorney general's refusal to change marriage law and a minister's claim of externally imposed same-sex marriage. A proposed gay tourism package drew opposition through the Barbados Nation newspaper's informal comment line.

Tourism marketing and legal reality diverge. The 'Welcome Stamp' visa markets openness to foreign remote workers, and its spouse rule was corrected to include same-sex spouses in July 2020, while employment discrimination against trans workers on grounds of presentation is described as routine and unremedied.

Trans Barbadians organise through BGLAD, founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed for education and public dialogue, and through NOW and veteran trans advocates who have run Trans Day of Remembrance vigils since 2017. Pride events have grown from a small gathering in November 2017 to a parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown, in July 2018.

Resident trans workers are not protected on grounds of gender identity or gender expression under the Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, according to Alexa D.V. Hoffmann, and firing or refusing to hire trans people for 'dressing wrong' is described as frequent. Residents have no route to legal gender recognition in the sourced material, no recognition of same-sex unions, and no adoption or surrogacy route as a couple. The Barbados Fertility Centre provides IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples; no equivalent service is documented for other family formations.

UGLAAB works on AIDS in the local LGBT community and said it would investigate the 2016 asylum-application allegations. UGLAAB and BGLAD have been the principal organisations in the local movement alongside trans advocates.
outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition and identity-document processes for trans people are not covered by the sourced material. Whether a change of marker is available through any administrative or judicial route is unresolved here, not established as absent.

No findings appear on access to transition-related healthcare, mental health or specialist care, nor on trans-specific custody, parental rights or family law outcomes. The only health-related provisions in the material are the Barbados Fertility Centre's IVF and artificial insemination for lesbian couples and UGLAAB's AIDS work.

No findings appear on the treatment of LGBT minors, detention of unaccompanied youth, or school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education. The only youth-adjacent legal detail is that under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, 'serious indecency' carried a maximum penalty of ten years in prison where the act was committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older.

The status of the September 2020 civil-union plan and the promised referendum is unresolved in the material, which predates any enactment. The outcome of the 2018 Inter-American Commission on Human Rights case over Sections 9 and 12 of the Sexual Offences Act is likewise unresolved, as is whether it proceeded to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights.
